item.title: The Psychology Explaining Why Bad Intentions Feel More Real
item.description:
Social Life

The Psychology Explaining Why Bad Intentions Feel More Real

Why forgetfulness feels intentional but kindness doesn't.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • We judge harmful side effects as intentional far more often than helpful ones.
  • This asymmetry shapes how suspicious or grateful we feel toward others.
  • Emotion, not logic, seems to drive which side effects feel deliberate.
  • Naming this bias won't erase it, but it can help us catch it in the moment.
The kind of gesture you almost don't notice was a choice.
Source: Clay Banks / Unsplash

The Numbers Don't Add Up

In a 2003 study by experimental philosopher Joshua Knobe, people read about a company chairman deciding on a new business plan (Knobe, 2003). He knew it would have a side effect on the environment, but that didn't factor into his decision; he just wanted the plan to increase profits.

Half the participants were told the side effect would harm the environment. Of those, 82 percent said the chairman did it intentionally. The other half were told the identical plan would help the environment instead. Only 23 percent said he helped it intentionally.

His reasoning never changed between the two versions. His indifference to the outcome never changed either. The only thing that moved was whether the outcome was good or bad, and that alone was nearly enough to flip the verdict.

Psychologists call this the Knobe effect: people are far more likely to judge a harmful side effect as intentional than an identical, equally unintended helpful one.

Why This Sounds Familiar

This phenomenon isn't confined to real or hypothetical CEOs. It shapes something much closer to home: how we read the people around us.

Picture a friend who's 30 minutes late and doesn't text. Something in you reaches for a reason almost immediately, and it usually isn't traffic. It's probably closer to the idea that they didn't think it mattered enough to alert you.

Now picture a different friend showing up early—and with coffee for you, because they remembered you'd had a hard week. That action rarely gets read as a decision at all; it just feels like something that happened to happen.

Same asymmetry. Different chairman.

Why Bad Intentions Stick and Good Ones Slide

A 2015 neuroimaging study helps explain this gap (Ngo et al., 2015). Researchers found two separate mechanisms doing the work: Harmful outcomes activate the amygdala, the brain's threat and emotion center, and that emotional charge is what makes an action feel deliberate. Helpful outcomes get routed through a region tied to weighing statistical norms instead, which tends to explain them away as circumstance rather than choice.

Harm registers as personal before any reasoning happens. Kindness has to argue its way into feeling personal, and it often loses that argument.

There's a second piece to this, from separate research on how these judgments actually form (Sripada & Konrath, 2011): People aren't carefully analyzing what someone was thinking in the moment. They're drawing on assumptions about the kind of person that someone already is. Distrust a friend a little, and her lateness confirms it. Trust her, and the same lateness barely registers.

What This Effect Does to Our Relationships

None of this stays in the lab.

A colleague who forgets to loop you in reads as careless, sometimes even hostile. A colleague who goes out of their way to include you reads as just doing their job. Suspicion comes cheap. Credit comes expensive.

Left alone, that asymmetry compounds. Relationships can end up running on a ledger where the bad columns fill in fast and the good ones stay strangely blank. That's not because the good things stop happening, but because our minds were never built to log them as intentional in the first place.

The Coffee, Revisited

Let's go back to the friend who showed up early with coffee. If the chairman's story teaches us anything, it's that she deserved more credit than she got in the moment, not because what she did was extraordinary, but because your mind was never built to log ordinary kindness as a choice someone made.

The late-arriving friend, on the other hand, may have deserved less certainty than you gave her. Traffic is a boring explanation. Carelessness is a much better story, the same way harm made a better story for 82 percent of Knobe's participants than help ever did.

Neither friend actually changed. What changed is knowing which of your verdicts came from evidence, and which came from the shape of the story your brain prefers to tell.

The forgetting rarely needed proof. The kindness usually does.

item.title: How to Deal With the "Crush Recession"
item.description:
Mating

How to Deal With the "Crush Recession"

There is a perception that people are losing enthusiasm for dating. Is it true?

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • "Crush recession" is a new slang term for a major downturn in enthusiasm about dating.
  • While a crush recession may leave a lot of pessimistic folks around you, try to stay open to possibilities.
  • Remain authentically yourself while adjusting your dating habits, expectations, and goals appropriately.
Source: Prostock-studio/Shutterstock

We may not be in an economic recession just yet. But GenZers and Millenials have been claiming on social media that a so-called "crush recession" has already emerged. It's a drop in "interest rates," meaning a major downturn in people's enthusiasm and optimism about having crushes — and in dating in general. Now, the term "crush recession" is not an official one by any means, and there's no official body that determines whether and when we enter such a recession and when you might want to put your love into a high-yield savings account as a precaution. Nevertheless, it does help to know when there is such a perception out there and what to do about it.

Is There Really a Crush Recession?

When it comes to economic recessions, in the U.S. the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) is the official arbiter. This body defines such a recession as a significant, widespread decline in economic activity that persists for more than a few months. If you are looking for a dating equivalent of the NBER, you'll be looking for a long time. There aren't measures such as nonfarm dating activity or number of times people are saying, "Do you like raisins? How about a date," to track dating enthusiasm. However, surveys have suggested that dating enthusiasm has indeed been dropping. For example, the 14th Annual "Singles In America” from 20205, a survey of 5,000 singles released by the Kinsey Institute in partnership with Match, found that 53% of singles reported dating burnout, 46% percent took breaks from dating to recharge, and 63% noticed more passivity in making the first move. Data have shown that dating app use and marriage rates have been falling as well.

What May Be Causing a Crush Recession

There are concrete reasons why there might be a so-called crush recession. One is right on the money. I've written previously about dateflation — how rising prices over the past year have made many aspects of dating a lot more expensive and thus less attractive. At the same time, stagnant wages, unemployment, or the lack of a steady income may be crushing the ability to cover these higher expenses.

Another thing being stressed on social media is the stress that's pervading much of the U.S. right now. A Gallup Poll showed that optimism among Americans in 2025 fell to a record low. And stress and pessimism can be like sweater vests when it comes to their effects on libido and attraction.

Then there's frustration with how dating works these days—troubling trends like dating app fatigue and the rise of situationships. The argument is that such trends have sucked the romance out of dating and made it seem more like shopping for toilet paper, underwear, or some other commodity. Swiping through a bunch of dating profiles that all seem to say the same thing — "fluent in sarcasm," "work hard, play hard," "I love to laugh," "partner in crime, "don't want drama" — can sort of swipe away one's enthusiasm for dating.

How a Crush Recession Might Affect Your Dating

So what then should you do about a crush recession, assuming that you don't have unilateral power to raise people's interest in dating? It does help to know that this may be going on so that you don't necessarily take any jaded and less-than-enthusiastic attitudes personally. Of course, it will remain important to distinguish between those who are a bit down on dating in general and those who are down on you specifically. Don't assume that when he or she says, "The bar was already on the floor, and you still showed up with a shovel," it's due simply to crush recession.

Remember: Any trend may not necessarily apply to you. Just look at economic downturns in the past. The Allstate company, for example, started during the Great Depression; Amgen, Genzyme, and MTV during the 1980s recession; and Slack, Uber, AirBnB, and WhatsApp during the 2008 recession.

In the same manner, cut yourself some "Slack" when it comes to dating, Just because many people around you may seem down on dating doesn't mean that any romantic attempt of yours will go down as well. Being pessimistic can become a sefl-sabotaging and self-fulfilling prophecy. Instead, stay open to possibilities and, as my medical school apartment-mate used to say, cautiously optimistic. You probably haven't heard too many people say, "Yeah, times were tough but what really got me through everything was my pessimism."

Make Appropriate Adjustments in Your Dating

This doesn't mean that you shouldn't make any adjustments in your dating approaches, though. Don't act like the main character on The Bachelor or The Bachelorette and assume that everyone else will automatically adapt to you. After all, during economic recessions, even Warren Buffet didn't stick to the same spending habits, expectations, and goals. Similarly, during a crush recession, while you shouldn't change who you fundamentally are, consider the following tweaks:

  • Opt for less expensive dates: Rather than breaking the bank, maybe go for a stroll along the river bank.
  • Change your expectations of dating: Again, don't expect people to be all hyped or amped up during dating. There may be some bumps and even some pessimism. So, don't fret if you and a date are not singing Taylor Swift's "Love Story" by the end of the night.
  • Change your goals for dating: Rather than being laser-focused on finding "The One," maybe your goal is more to simply meet and learn about different people. In the meantime, you might find that the right match for you comes in an expected package.

Again, it will be more important than ever to say authentic so you don't waste time and energy with the wrong people. But these tweaks can help keep interest rates high, so to speak. Plus, you never know: Someone you may not have any interest in initially may end up crushing it.

item.title: When "Almost Unavailable" Becomes Something More
item.description:
Fantasies

When "Almost Unavailable" Becomes Something More

Some fantasies actually help us grow.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Not every fantasy pulls us away from reality; some can help us grow.
  • You don't have to act on a crush for it to have psychological meaning.
  • Living with uncertainty can sometimes be healthier than rushing to closure.
  • Sometimes what stays with us isn't the person, but the possibility they awakened.

In part 1 of this series, we looked at why "almost unavailable" people are so captivating — how someone who stays just out of reach can come to carry our idealised projections, and how the Zeigarnik effect, uncertain reward prediction, and Lacan's idea of symbolic representation all help keep that possibility open rather than closed.

So is this kind of unresolved longing just an illusion destined to fade, or can it be something more—a psychologically meaningful space in its own right?

British psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott offered a concept that helps make sense of this unresolved pull: potential space. He argued that people don't only live in fantasy or in reality; between the two lies a creative space. This is where children play, where art happens, and where we can lose ourselves completely while reading a novel or watching a film.

In this space, we know something hasn't happened yet, but we allow ourselves to imagine that it might; we know the story may never reach an ending, yet we're still willing to let it go on existing.

The "almost unavailable" figures may be the ones most able to keep a relationship suspended in this potential space. Because the relationship never truly enters reality, the fantasy doesn't need to face reality's test right away. We keep imagining, keep projecting, keep giving the relationship new meaning. What truly brings us joy, sometimes, isn't the everyday life that follows getting what we want, but a future that still holds infinite possibility.

This has made me rethink my own past writing on fantasy.

Over the years, I've mostly discussed how fantasy sustains psychological pathology. When someone keeps using fantasy to escape reality, letting reality give way to the imagined self that will never come true, fantasy can indeed become a defense — one that keeps a person trapped in pain, unable to keep growing.

But while writing this piece, I've felt that this is only one side of fantasy.

For a long time, we've tended to treat fantasy as the opposite of reality, as if a mature person should become steadily more "grounded," with less and less room for fantasy.

But perhaps a truly mature person isn't someone without fantasy, but someone who can let fantasy stay in its place as fantasy, while still allowing it to nourish reality.

A high-schooler preparing for medical school might fantasise about the day they'll wear a white coat. A young researcher might imagine standing on stage at an international conference one day. A student just starting university might, because they admire a teaching assistant, begin to think about who they want to become in the future.

These fantasies aren't a way of fleeing reality. On the contrary, they offer a temporary psychological space that lets us keep trying on different versions of ourselves, gradually growing toward the self we haven't yet become.

And so, fantasy is not the opposite of reality. When fantasy stays connected to reality, it can become a driving force for reality's own development. A student might stay more engaged in class because they admire a teaching assistant. A young researcher might push harder in a particular direction because they imagine themselves as a rising star in the field.

Fantasy hasn't taken them away from reality. On the contrary, it has given reality a direction.

So maturity isn't necessarily giving up fantasy but learning to live alongside it in peace.

Of course, real-world boundaries must be respected. A professional ethic exists between teaching assistants and students, and it should never develop into an actual intimate relationship. But fantasy itself doesn't necessarily need to be extinguished. A student can study harder because they admire a teaching assistant; can rethink their own future because they want to become someone like him; can, through a relationship that never truly began, experience for the first time what it feels like to genuinely admire someone, to idealise them, to feel that flutter of the heart.

Desire can exist. So can boundaries. Fantasy doesn't need to be eliminated, or realised, in order to help a person grow.

British psychoanalyst Wilfred Bion was preoccupied with one question: Can a person bear "not knowing"?

When we like someone, we always want an answer as fast as possible: "Does he actually like me?" "Do we have a chance?" "Should I tell him now?" So we rush to define the relationship, rush to find an answer, rush to end this uncomfortable uncertainty.

But Bion, borrowing the poet John Keats's idea of negative capability, points us toward another possibility: Maturity isn't about arriving at an answer right away. It's the capacity to let a question go unanswered for a while — to keep thinking, keep feeling, inside that uncertainty, instead of rushing to turn everything into something fixed and certain.

Looking back at those "almost unavailable" people, perhaps what truly draws us to them isn't only who they are, but the fact that they keep a question permanently open: "If we had met at a different stage of our lives, would the ending have been different?" "If I had said it out loud back then, what would have happened?" "If we hadn't been teacher and student, or colleagues, or two people who simply arrived in each other's lives a little too late — would the story have turned out completely differently?"

These questions may never have answers. But it's exactly because of that, that they keep pushing us to think about what we truly want, and who we hope to become.

Psychology theories explain why this kind of relationship so easily seizes our attention. Lacan explains why it can carry such rich desire. Winnicott reminds us that fantasy isn't only an escape from reality; it can also become a space for personal development. And Bion, in turn, tells us that what truly matters may not be knowing the answer as quickly as possible, but allowing a question to remain open for a while.

These aren't competing theories. They describe the same relationship structure.

Perhaps what truly draws us to "almost unavailable" people was never the promise that it would become love. It's that it keeps the future open.

And within that possibility that hasn't yet been closed off, we slowly discover who we truly want to become.

item.title: Are You the Invisible Patient?
item.description:
Caregiving

Are You the Invisible Patient?

When medical tragedy happens to a loved one, it happens to you, too.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Millions of critical illness survivors leave U.S. hospitals to be cared for by their own informal system.
  • With little guidance, patients’ loved ones often assume overwhelming caregiving responsibilities.
  • These "co-survivors" need support to ensure positive medical outcomes and to address their own trauma.
Present yet often unseen, the invisible patient carries the emotional weight of a loved one's medical crisis.
Source: Sarah Holmlund / Shutterstock

by Jennifer Chap, BS and Patricia O'Gorman, Ph.D.

We all live interconnected in families, friendships, communities, within our own unique social systems. So, when tragedy happens to someone in our life, we feel it.

Whether you are a passerby who sees a neighbor collapse, calls 9-1-1, and begins CPR, a parent whose teenager is in the ER after a crash, or the partner of someone who is critically ill in the ICU, you are affected. You may feel shock, your heart racing as fear and uncertainty take hold. You are the “invisible patient” feeling alone and suffering in silence.

We are all connected

Immediately, you face many decisions about your responsibilities—children, work, pets—so you can be with your loved one.

Eventually, they will hopefully be discharged home, but that may be just a new beginning.

Once discharged, your loved one’s care falls to you to manage, support, and champion, while continuing to function in other areas of your life.

You are more than a caregiver

We often use the term “caregiver” for this new status, but “caregiver” does not go far enough. You and your loved one experienced the medical event from different perspectives. Your loved one is the survivor. And you are the co-survivor.

Co-survivor is a powerful new identifier that makes you visible to yourself and others. It empowers you to see your own trauma stemming from your loved one’s medical challenges. You may need support to stay healthy for yourself, your survivor, and the other loved ones in your life.

Finding your new normal

For many, the co-survivor job description looks something like this:

  • Manage medications
  • Care for surgical wounds
  • Monitor vitals
  • Schedule appointments, transport, and handle insurance
  • Manage nutrition
  • Lift, dress, shower, etc.
  • Problem-solve and encourage

This is daunting. But science-backed support models can guide your next steps in caring for your own needs so that you can care for your loved one.

Below are two support systems: one new, the other 75 years old. The development of both included people with lived experience.

Cardiac arrest can affect anyone

The world was shocked in 2023 when Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin collapsed on the field in sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) on live TV. Coaches, players, fans, and 23 million viewers watched in horror as staff performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and used an automatic external defibrillator (AED) to resuscitate him.

What most don’t realize: SCA strikes 1,000 people outside of U.S. hospitals daily, yet only one in 10 survives (Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival [CARES], 2026). Survival depends on bystander action: calling 9-1-1 , starting CPR immediately, and, if available, applying an AED. Often, family members become lay rescuers, as most SCAs (71%) happen at home.

For decades, the aftermath of SCA went unrecognized, leaving those affected to process this existential experience alone. Recently, the medical community made a major shift in acknowledging SCA's impact. In 2020, the American Heart Association published a groundbreaking statement on SCA survivorship, identifying the need for post-hospital-discharge physical, cognitive, and psychological support for survivors and co-survivors, as well as bereaved families and lay rescuers (Sawyer et al., 2020).

Among co-survivors, the greatest unmet need is information about cardiac arrest, per an NIH-supported study of 550 co-survivors (Agarwal, Chap et al., 2024a). This echoes the broader lack of public awareness and understanding around SCA, CPR, and AEDs (Newman, Chap et al., 2018).

Discovering this gap led to the creation of free online educational resources. One such resource connects co-survivors affected by this life-altering event to trusted information that orients and empowers them (Resuscitation Council US, 2023). Co-designed by healthcare professionals, researchers, and people with lived experience, informational blog-like articles combine lay-friendly information with insights from co-survivors who lived it.

Since launching in 2023, this resource has reached 80,000-plus people in more than 200 countries. Preliminary NIH-supported trial data show that, three months post-discharge, co-survivors who used it had significantly less uncertainty, fewer PTSD symptoms, and lower caregiver burden than those receiving standard care (Agarwal et al., 2024b).

SCA and addiction are surprisingly connected

A striking statistic is that adults who overdosed represented 4.5% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in the U.S. in 2025 (CARES, 2026). This figure jumps to 27% among young adults aged 19-34.

But the overdoses, car crashes, and organ failures are often preceded by years of co-survivors witnessing someone they care about becoming more and more ill with a variety of health issues, as they scramble to try to keep their loved one together.

Importantly, these co-survivors have an advantage in tapping resources that have been developing for the past 75 years.

Al-Anonoffers free 24/7 in-person and virtual support groups in over 100 countries and literature for adults and teens affected by a loved one’s addiction, be it a parent, sibling, partner, child, or friend. Al–Anon was founded 75 years ago by individuals with lived experience, impacted by the addiction of a loved one. They realized that they needed support from others who understood this. They developed mutual support groups of peers who share their experience, strength, and hope in facing the challenges of co-survivorship.

Meetings offer a highly structured discussion, led by a group member, not a mental health professional. Each participant, in turn, shares on the topic being discussed. There is no crosstalk—that is, no conversation. Instead, there is personal sharing on a topic (O'Gorman, 2024). This produces validation of an individual’s experience, in which the healing power of being seen and understood by others who have had similar experiences reduces shame and isolation (The Lancet Respiratory Medicine, 2026).

Does it work? Al–Anon has been conducting member research for over 40 years. In their 2024 survey, Al–Anon found that 80% of respondents reported improved mental health within the first year (Al–Anon Family Group Headquarters, Inc., 2024). Among those attending four years or more, this figure jumps to 91%. These results indicate that supporting co-survivors is effective.

Moving forward

If you are a co-survivor, understand that you have been invisible for too long. Realize that you deserve support—in fact, you need it. Seek out information and community that can be accessed in person, virtually, or online.

You were never just a caregiver. You are a co-survivor—in it together with your loved one, hand in hand.

Source: Jennifer Chap

The co-authors co-chair the HOPE Critical Care Collaborative (Trauma Division, APA).

Jennifer Chap, BS, is a co-survivor/lay rescuer whose husband survived SCA. She is a speaker, author, and researcher, and a founding member of Heartsight and a member of the Medical Trauma Recovery Alliance. She also chairs the Orange County (Florida) CPR AED subcommittee and co-founded BuddyCPR and StrataVerve, a strategic marketing practice.

Source: Patricia O'Gorman, PhD

Patricia O’Gorman, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist with a virtual practice, a trauma and addiction specialist, a life coach, and the author of nine books, numerous articles, and an international speaker. She is co-founder and Advisory Board Member of The National Association for Children of Addiction.
